pr_title: Dockershim: Execute sandbox with less privileges
pr_body:
**What type of PR is this?**
/kind bug

**What this PR does / why we need it**:
Decreases the sandbox's attack surface by running it with `no-new-privileges` and with its own optimised seccomp profile.

As a side effect, it allows end users to set seccomp profiles at pod level with the same profile as they would for container level, considering the pod only has containers with `AllowPrivilegeEscalation=false`. 

Without this PR users had to whitelist some syscalls regardless of their containers needing them: `capset`, `set_tid_address`, `setgid`, `setgroups`, `setuid` and etc. More information and examples at #84623.

**Which issue(s) this PR fixes**:
Fixes #84623 (for dockershim)


**Special notes for your reviewer**:
Feature parity with other runtimes will be done through a different PR. 

**Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?**:
```release-note
dockershim security: pod sandbox now runs with `no-new-privileges` and with its own seccomp profile
dockershim seccomp: custom profiles can now have smaller footprints when set at pod level with containers using AllowPrivilegeEscalation=false
```

**Additional documentation e.g., KEPs (Kubernetes Enhancement Proposals), usage docs, etc.**:
```docs
NONE
```

/cc @tallclair @Random-Liu
/sig node
pr_comments: I wonder whether it would be worth adding a flag to allow administrators to overwrite the sandbox seccomp profile at kubelet startup time.

issue_context.title: Seccomp at POD level always requires too many syscalls
issue_context.body:
**What happened**: For a single container pod with `AllowPrivilegeEscalation=false`, setting the seccomp profile at pod or container level results in vastly different syscalls to be whitelisted. **What you expected to happen**: The same (or similar) pod seccomp profile should work at both container or pod levels. Instead, setting profiles at pod level requires excessive permissions, including: `capset`, `set_tid_address`, `setgid`, `setgroups` and `setuid`. The table below shows what syscalls must be whitelisted to run a simple pod depending on whether the seccomp profile is set at pod or container level: | Seccomp set at | Whitelisted syscalls | |------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------| | Container Level | arch_prctl
brk
close
execve
exit_group
futex
mprotect
nanosleep
stat
write | | Pod Level | **access**
arch_prctl
brk
**capget**
**capset**
**chdir**
close
**epoll_ctl**
**epoll_pwait**
execve
exit_group
**fchown**
**fcntl**
**fstat**
**fstatfs**
futex
**getcwd**
**getdents64**
**getgid**
getpid
**getppid**
**getuid**
**lstat**
mprotect
nanosleep
**newfstatat**
**openat**
**pause**
**prctl**
**read**
**readlink**
**rt_sigaction**
**rt_sigprocmask**
**set_tid_address**
**setgid**
**setgroups**
**setuid**
**statfs**
stat
**uname**
**wait4**
write | The reason for this behaviour seems to be that when seccomp profiles are applied at pod level it is applied to all containers, including the "pause" container. The problem is that this container always run with `AllowPrivilegeEscalation=true`, which makes the container runtime (docker at least) to apply the seccomp early in the process leading to an increased profile footprint. Forcing the "pause" container to run with `AllowPrivilegeEscalation=false` (through changes on the source code) results in a lighter seccomp profile: arch_prctl
brk
close
execve
exit_group
futex
mprotect
nanosleep
stat
write
**uname**
**pause**
**rt_sigaction** However, refraining from applying the seccomp profile to the "pause" container allows for the exact same profile to work at both levels. Would there be a problem to either: 1) Change the pause container to not apply the seccomp profile (preferable)? 2) Allow a setting for the pause container to have its `AllowPrivilegeEscalation` configurable? **How to reproduce it**: 1. Spin up a kubernetes cluster with `hack/local-up-cluster.sh` 2. Place the contents of both `*.json` files into `/var/lib/kubelet/seccomp/` 3. Create the pods defined on `pods.yaml` file 4. Confirm that only the pod pod-level-container-perms is **not** running ```console $ kubectl get pods -n default NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS AGE container-level 1/1 Running 0 7s pod-level-container-perms 0/1 ContainerCreating 0 7s pod-level-excessive-perms 1/1 Running 0 7s ``` #### Example Files **pods.yaml**: ```yaml apiVersion: v1 kind: Pod metadata: name: container-level annotations: container.seccomp.security.alpha.kubernetes.io/container-level: 'localhost/container-profile.json' spec: containers: - name: container-level image: alpine command: ["sh"] args: ["-c", "echo hi && sleep 120"] securityContext: allowPrivilegeEscalation: false --- apiVersion: v1 kind: Pod metadata: name: pod-level-excessive-perms annotations: seccomp.security.alpha.kubernetes.io/pod: 'localhost/pod-profile.json' spec: containers: - name: pod-level-excessive-perms image: alpine command: ["sh"] args: ["-c", "echo hi && sleep 120"] securityContext: allowPrivilegeEscalation: false --- apiVersion: v1 kind: Pod metadata: name: pod-level-container-perms annotations: seccomp.security.alpha.kubernetes.io/pod: 'localhost/container-profile.json' spec: containers: - name: pod-level-container-perms image: alpine command: ["sh"] args: ["-c", "echo hi && sleep 120"] securityContext: allowPrivilegeEscalation: false ``` **container-profile.json** ```json { "defaultAction": "SCMP_ACT_ERRNO", "architectures": [ "SCMP_ARCH_X86_64", "SCMP_ARCH_X86", "SCMP_ARCH_X32" ], "syscalls": [ { "names": [ "arch_prctl", "brk", "close", "execve", "exit_group", "futex", "mprotect", "nanosleep", "stat", "write" ], "action": "SCMP_ACT_ALLOW" } ] } ``` **pod-profile.json** ```json { "defaultAction": "SCMP_ACT_ERRNO", "architectures": [ "SCMP_ARCH_X86_64", "SCMP_ARCH_X86", "SCMP_ARCH_X32" ], "syscalls": [ { "names": [ "arch_prctl", "brk", "capget", "capset", "chdir", "close", "execve", "exit_group", "fstat", "fstatfs", "futex", "getdents64", "getppid", "lstat", "mprotect", "nanosleep", "newfstatat", "openat", "prctl", "read", "rt_sigaction", "statfs", "setgid", "setgroups", "setuid", "stat", "uname", "write" ], "action": "SCMP_ACT_ALLOW" } ] } ``` **Anything else we need to know?**: This can be reproduced with both dockershim and cri-o runtime. **Environment**: runC and kubelet were the latest from master: ``` $ runc -v [HEAD] runc version spec: 1.0.1-dev $ kubelet --version Kubernetes v1.18.0-alpha.0.642+0968636760dae2 $ docker version Client: Version: 18.09.7 API version: 1.39 Go version: go1.10.1 Git commit: 2d0083d Built: Fri Aug 16 14:20:06 2019 OS/Arch: linux/amd64 Experimental: false Server: Engine: Version: 18.09.7 API version: 1.39 (minimum version 1.12) Go version: go1.10.1 Git commit: 2d0083d Built: Wed Aug 14 19:41:23 2019 OS/Arch: linux/amd64 Experimental: false $ crio -h VERSION: 1.17.0-dev commit: "6ea0e8c807d52a30863f8f8a05272e0d4028c7f9" ``` /area security /cc @tallclair /assign @pjbgf /sig node
comments: On a fresh install the issue is reproducible in both dockershim and cri-o.

> Forcing the "pause" container to run with AllowPrivilegeEscalation=false (through changes on the source code) results in a lighter seccomp profile

I think we can always set `AllowPrivilegeEscalation=false` for pause container.

And for pause container, I think it makes sense to set a default seccomp profile inside the container runtime? It seems that the seccomp profile for pause container shouldn't be configurable by users, because the behavior is fixed for a dedicated pause container image, we know exactly what it needs.

@pjbgf Can you explain why `AllowPrivilegeEscalation` would change the syscall requirement? Not sure how it works.

That's awesome, @Random-Liu, thank you. I will give it a go on a PR for that.

> @pjbgf Can you explain why `AllowPrivilegeEscalation` would change the syscall requirement? Not sure how it works.

Historically, Docker always applied the seccomp profile very early in the process of starting  containers, which meant that things such as drop caps and setuid had to be included in the users seccomp profile. From version 1.12, they added the option of executing it as the very last thing just before the `exec` when `AllowPrivilegeEscalation=true`.

In runC, when `AllowPrivilegeEscalation=true`, seccomp is applied before [finalizeNamespace](https://github.com/opencontainers/runc/blob/b133feaeeb2e69ba94aa95eac3a455a143435ea9/libcontainer/init_linux.go#L122) which handles capabilities, setuid/setgid, etc:
https://github.com/opencontainers/runc/blob/b133feaeeb2e69ba94aa95eac3a455a143435ea9/libcontainer/standard_init_linux.go#L156

Otherwise it happens here:

review_comments: How did you come up with this list of syscalls? Was it through static or dynamic analysis?

It was a combination of both. I started with a static analysis using https://github.com/pjbgf/gosystract, which goes through all syscalls in the possible execution paths for the go binary and its dependencies. Then incremented it by using dynamic analysis with another tool I built which is not yet public.
I'd like to put this behind a feature gate, so it's easier to roll back if needed. It might be good to start in alpha too, to enable more time for soak testing.

I will add the feature gate today. Are you OK with the name and default values as per below?

```golang
PodSandboxSeccomp = false
```
Is this only used by docker? Maybe it should be moved to the dockershim package in that case?
Currently yes, but once the CRI api is changed, this would also be used there.
@tallclair yes, it needs to in order to decrease the amount of required permissions. The runtimes tend to have a small permission requirement when executed with 'no-new-privs' on.
What's the plan for containerd / cri-o? I assume the a similar change needs to be merged into those repos? Or can we control the infra container for remote runtimes from within the Kubelet?
I believe we can do it within the kubelet. Let me go through this later on and get back to you.

We can only partially do this from the Kubelet. For sandboxes, we can only use seccomp paths using the current syntax: `runtime/name` or `localhost/name`. We cannot provide the full seccomp json. To use the custom profile created on this PR for non dockershim, we would have to ensure the profile is written on disk and refer to it with the `localhost` prefix. However, that would still not work, because we would need to pass on the `no-new-privilege` flag, which I believe we currently can only do for the "normal containers".

For those reasons, the Alpha version defaults the sandbox container seccomp profile to `runtime/default` when using non dockershim runtimes. The end result is the same, users will be able to interchance their container and pod level profiles with least privileges. However, sandboxes running in dockershim will operate at tighter security profiles.

The longer term of this could be a new built-in profile type `kubernetes/sandbox` plus changes on the CRI API for the no-new-priv flag.

The kubelet doesn't actually have any knowledge of the infra container when interacting with the CRI directly - the sandbox could be anything. So, the fact that containerd & cri-o are running the pause container is really an implementation detail of those runtimes, and I think this change needs to be baked into those runtimes.

Given that, I think the best way to handle this would be to add this profile as a library alongside the pause source: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/tree/master/build/pause, and then import the profile to dockershim, as well as containerd & cri-o. Ideally, profile could just be a json file in the paues directory, but I'm not sure what the best way to turn that into a go importable library are.

@tallclair you are absolutely right. I will take this into consideration and see how we can bridge that gap before making seccomp GA. I have a few ideas and will explore them on tomorrow's call. I will forward you the details, in case you are available then.
